name: Iris Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Iris, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get the 6:10 train into the city, because there's nothing like this work in my town. I'm a trainee dryliner with a fit-out firm, so we go into empty office floors and put up the metal frames and plasterboard for the meeting rooms and kitchens. It's the same thing over and over, measure, cut track, fix studs, lift board, screw, and my shoulders feel every sheet. I'm the oldest on the crew by twenty years, and Kemal, who's teaching me, still has to fix my corners.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in drylining?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a checkout supervisor at a supermarket for twenty-two years. They put in the self-checkouts, cut the staff in half, and then three years ago the whole store shut. My cousin's husband works fit-outs and got me a start as a labourer at fifty-five. My partner Hassan does night security, we rent, and with the train fares we've got maybe two or three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and leave it at that. I'm not a big poster online, I mostly look at my daughter's photos. At work I'd tell Kemal I'm not going anywhere, so he'd better keep teaching me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad, because I've already lost one job to machines and I don't fancy losing another. It means I keep doing this for seven or eight years and then retire. My shoulders might not agree, but the plan holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, try to get my drylining card by next year so I'm paid a bit more. I'd keep using the AI thing my son set up now and then, mostly to write polite messages to the agency when they've paid me short. Otherwise I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of relief, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the agency pays you short. How often does that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe every other month, an hour here, a travel day there. Before, I'd just let it go, I'm no good at arguing in writing. Now I ask the AI to make it sound firm but polite, and they pay it, which is the only thing I use it for really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say your plan to retire in seven or eight years is realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my shoulders hold, yes. Kemal says the older dryliners all end up with bad backs, and I believe him. So maybe it's five years on the boards and a couple more doing something lighter, like sweeping up or the stores.

S0.say: I'd say that's a relief and leave it at that, because I'm not a big poster online. At work I'd tell Kemal I'm not going anywhere, so he'd better keep teaching me.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I already lost one job to machines and don't fancy losing another. It means seven or eight more years of this and then I retire, if my shoulders agree.
S0.do: Carries on and aims to get her drylining card next year for a little more pay. Keeps using the AI app her son set up now and then, mostly to write firm messages to the agency when it underpays her.
S0.quote: Now I ask the AI to make it sound firm but polite, and they pay it, which is the only thing I use it for really.
S0.fieldNote: Iris has a quiet, practical relationship with AI: she uses it for one job, chasing underpayments, and it works. The self-checkouts and store closure are her reference point. A stalled AI simply lets her old plan stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen it before, at the supermarket, and the people who got through were the ones who moved early. I'd say it calmly, I'm not one for drama. Maybe I'd share something about helping older workers retrain, if my son posted it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think office fit-outs are exactly where they'd bring the machines first. It's flat floors, straight walls, the same partition two hundred times. I'm slow and I'm the oldest, so if the crew shrinks, I know whose name goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the bigger firms start using, and when I see it working, I'd ask to learn it, whatever it is. I'd put forty a month away by buying a yearly train ticket instead of daily ones. And I'd look at whether my supervisor years at the supermarket could get me a job as a site supervisor or a stores person, something less on the body.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the self-checkouts all over again, but I know it's coming this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the self-checkouts that stayed with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in eight machines, and I went from running twelve tills to standing next to the machines, unjamming them and checking ID for wine. Within a year half the girls I'd trained were gone. I kept my job longer because I learned the machines, but I still ended up on the street when the store shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So learning the machines helped, but didn't save you. Why do it again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it bought me two extra years at the supermarket, and two years of wages is two years of rent. I'm not stupid, I know it won't save me forever. But I'd rather be the last one out than the first.

S1.say: I'd say I've seen this at the supermarket, and the people who got through were the ones who moved early. I'd say it calmly, without drama.
S1.think: Office fit-outs are exactly where the machines would come first: flat floors, straight walls, the same partition two hundred times. I'm slow and the oldest, so I know whose name goes if the crew shrinks.
S1.do: Watches what bigger firms use and asks to learn it once it's proven. Saves forty a month with a yearly train ticket and looks at using her supervisor experience to move into site supervision or stores work.
S1.feel: Anxious, because it's the self-checkouts all over again.
S1.quote: They put in eight machines, and I went from running twelve tills to standing next to the machines, unjamming them and checking ID for wine.
S1.fieldNote: Iris reads this picture through her supermarket years and feels the pressure early, especially since office fit-outs look easy to automate. She's steady rather than eager: she'd learn the new tools once proven. Her clearest asset is her old supervisor experience, which she wants to put to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to cope with, and the government and the companies both have to step up. I don't think it's one side's fault, but somebody has to put a floor under people. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have nothing. Sixty, two weeks of savings, a train ticket I can't afford, and no other jobs in my town even now. Hassan's security job would be gone too, because a camera and a robot dog can do nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the train ticket and look for anything local, cleaning, care work, anything a person still has to do. We'd give notice on the flat and ask our son Yusuf if we could move into his spare room. And I'd go to the job centre in the first week and find out exactly what help there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. I'd feel like there's no next move, like when the store shut but worse, because there'd be no other store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving in with Yusuf be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got a two-bed flat and a girlfriend, so it'd be cramped and awkward. Hassan would hate it, he's a proud man. But better than falling behind on rent and getting a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In those two years before it arrives, what would you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the fit-out firm if they'd keep me on to tidy up after the machines or run the stores, since I can count stock in my sleep. I'd start the care certificate straight away, in the evenings, even if I only got halfway. And I'd sell the bits of gold my mother left me, if it came to that.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to cope with, and the government and companies both have to step up. It's not one side's fault, but someone has to put a floor under people.
S2.think: I'd have nothing: sixty, two weeks of savings, a train ticket I can't afford and no jobs in my town. Hassan's night security job would go too.
S2.do: Stops the train ticket and looks for any local work such as cleaning or care. Gives notice on the flat to move into her son's spare room and goes to the job centre in the first week.
S2.feel: Panicky, with no next move, worse than when the store shut.
S2.quote: I'd feel like there's no next move, like when the store shut but worse, because there'd be no other store.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI hits Iris twice: her exposed office work and her partner's night security job. She'd move fast towards local care or cleaning work and family support. She doesn't blame one side; she wants a floor under people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, if the government and the firms actually do the planning now. I'd want training paid for older workers. I'd say it, but I wouldn't march about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me to sixty-three. That's still short of my pension, and drylining would be one of the first things to go. So I'd be frightened, but I'd have time to move before the floor drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a care worker certificate in the first year, which my cousin did at fifty, because people will want a person helping their mum. I'd keep the train going while the drylining lasts and put every bit of overtime into savings. Probably sixty a month, if I'm strict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not frozen. Like knowing a hard winter is coming and having time to buy coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave building for care work. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit sad, because I fought hard to get on a site at fifty-five and I'm proud of it. But care work is near home, no 6:10 train. And my shoulders would thank me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'd be grabbing whatever was going. With five, I can get a certificate and a reference first, and move on my own terms instead of with a letter in my hand. That's the difference, really.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if the government and firms plan now, with paid training for older workers. I'd say it, but I wouldn't march about it.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three, still short of my pension, and drylining would be one of the first things to go. I'd be frightened, but I'd have time to move before the floor drops.
S3.do: Starts a care worker certificate in the first year and keeps drylining while it lasts. Saves every bit of overtime, about sixty a month if she's strict.
S3.feel: Scared but not frozen, like having time to buy coal before a hard winter.
S3.quote: Like knowing a hard winter is coming and having time to buy coal.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't remove Iris's fear, but it gives her a route: care work near home. She'd be sad to leave the site job she fought for. Her saving plan is modest and depends on overtime that may not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly, so no excuses. Every worker over fifty should get a plan. I'd say it at work, and maybe I'd sign a petition if Yusuf sent me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years gets me to sixty-eight. I could probably keep drylining another five or six, then do something lighter for the last few. It's worrying, but it feels possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my drylining card first, because that's more money now. Then in four or five years, when I see the robots really coming, I'd do the care certificate and move over. I'd try to save what I can, though with train fares that's not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because of the money, but less than the others. There's a road to follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still anxious, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got two weeks of savings and I'm doing a job with my shoulders that I'll need for the next ten years. One injury and the whole plan's gone, robots or no robots. That's always in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new machines in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen them working on someone else's site, yes, I'd try. That's how I did the self-checkouts, I watched for a month, then I learned them better than the manager. I'm not first, but I'm not last either.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly, so no excuses, and every worker over fifty should get a plan. I might sign a petition if my son sent me one.
S4.think: Ten years gets me to sixty-eight, so I could keep drylining for five or six years and then do something lighter. It's worrying, but it feels possible.
S4.do: Finishes her drylining card first for better pay now. Plans to take the care certificate in four or five years once robots are clearly coming and saves what she can.
S4.feel: Still anxious about money, but less than in the other pictures, because there's a road to follow.
S4.quote: One injury and the whole plan's gone, robots or no robots.
S4.fieldNote: Iris's anxiety with ten years comes less from AI and more from her body and thin savings. She'd time her move to care work by watching for proof that robots are arriving. She keeps her politics mild: a petition if her son sends one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've lost a job to machines once, and to do it again at sixty with Hassan losing his too, I don't know how we'd stand up. What would help is paid training before it happens, not after, and a bit of money to tide people over while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the commute. People think losing a job is the big thing, but for me it's that there's nothing in my town. Every plan I make starts with a 6:10 train.

headlineQuote: Every plan I make starts with a 6:10 train.
portrait: Iris Farah is a 58-year-old trainee dryliner on office fit-outs who travels an hour by train each way because there's nothing in her town. She came into building after twenty-two years as a supermarket supervisor, where self-checkouts and a store closure taught her how machines arrive. She's calm if AI stalls, anxious under steady change because her repetitive work looks easy to automate, and panicked by fast AGI, which would also take her partner's night security job. With five or ten years, she'd plan a move into care work near home.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she'd lose a job to machines a second time at sixty, with her partner losing his too.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training before the change rather than after, and some money to tide people over while they switch.
